newsitem.title: USA: High prices seen limiting Kansas wheat abandonment.
newsitem.headline: High prices seen limiting Kansas wheat abandonment.

text.p: High wheat prices and limitations caused by the spring application of herbicides should limit abandonment of wheat in Kansas following last weekend's freeze, experts said.

"We have a spring wheat crop that is in danger because of flooding in the northern plains, and the price of wheat is high," said Lynn Rundle, chief executive of the 21st Century Alliance, a group of 700 Kansas wheat producers.
"That is going to motivate some producers to let it grow and see what happens," he said.
He said Kansas abandonment should be less than in 1996 when farmers gave up on three million acres due to drought.

"It is too early to tell (the level of abandonment) but my guess is it sure won't be three million. When you drive up the price of wheat a buck in three or four days, that 40-bushel (an acre) crop that turned into 25 doesn't look that bad," Rundle said.
Jim Shroyer, extension agronomist at Kansas State University, said spring application of herbicides would limit farmers' ability to switch to alternative crops such as sorghum, corn and sunflowers.
"This year the wheat looked good so they put on the herbicide," Shroyer said. "The more commonly used (herbicides) have the more severe planting restrictions. Their hands are tied."
Shroyer said herbicide application had been heaviest in the "central corridor of the state." He also noted high prices would limit abandonment.

"There will be a lot of wheat which in a normal year would have been cast aside, which because of the market, because of the limitations of what they can do, they will leave it," Kansas State's Shroyer said.
Shroyer also said farmers did not need to make a quick decision and should wait until the extent of damage becomes clearer, possibly around the middle of next week.
"They have a month (to make a decision) on corn. For beans they have got (even) longer," he said.

New crop July hard red winter wheat futures on the Kansas City Board of Trade hit a nine-month high on Tuesday, peaking at $4.55 a bushel, a climb of about 75 cents since cold weather forecasts began to circulate in early April.
At 1220 CDT Wednesday the July contract was trading down 9-3/4 cents a bushel on the day at $4.38.
